newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. allies press Washington on U.N. debt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. allies press Washington on U.N. debt.

text.p: European allies stepped up the pressure on Tuesday for the United States to pay its huge debts to the United Nations, saying that the world body's crippling financial crisis could not go on.

Washington owes some $1.6 billion, more than half of the debt mountain that has pushed the United Nations close to bankruptcy. The United States has said there must be more radical reforms before it meets its commitments in full.
U.S. President Bill Clinton promised on Tuesday that Washington would pay up.
But European allies speaking at the U.N. General Assembly in New York said those countries owing money to the United Nations should pay immediately -- and without conditions.
Ireland, speaking on behalf of the 15-nation European Union, said efforts to reform the United Nations were taking place "against the backdrop of a serious financial crisis."
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring did not mention the United States by name but told the U.N. assembly:
"All member states have an obligation to discharge their arrears...promptly, in full and without conditions."
His comments were echoed by British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
"All members must pay what they owe...and promptly. The UN faces a critical year...This year must see a solution to the financial crisis," Rifkind said.

On Monday, Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland -- often mentioned as a potential candidate for U.N. secretary-general -- went even further. She bluntly told the assembly that refusal to pay dues amounted to intimidation.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov talked of the need for U.N. reform but did not address the debt question. After the United States, Russia is the biggest debtor, owing more than $335 million.
Alluding to hostility towards the United Nations in the Republican-dominated U.S. Congress, Clinton blamed opponents for difficulties in paying the country's bill.
"We are paying our dues and we are committed to paying off our accrued obligations soon," Clinton told the assembly.

Discussions on reforming the payments system for member states have made little progress since world nations called for changes at last year's celebrations to mark the 50th anniversary of the United Nations.

The financial crisis comes at a time of uncertainty about the U.N.'s future role after the failure of its peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and Somalia. Discussion on other reforms of the U.N. system has also made little headway.
Since Washington has blocked the appointment of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali for a second five-year term, it is also unclear who will lead the United Nations into the 21st century.
